note: Phase 2 priority sources plus democracy spine and community-safety/justice sources (COPS, DOJ private prisons 2016/2017, BJA, NIJ). No fabricated findings. Secondary sources labeled.

sources.title: Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2019 to 2022: Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances
authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
sources.summary: Triennial SCF results: real median net worth rose 37% to $192,900 (2022); real mean net worth rose 23% to $1,063,700. Patterns imply some narrowing of the wealth distribution between 2019 and 2022 while levels remain highly unequal (mean far above median).
key_findings: Median net worth $192,900 in 2022 (2022 dollars)
Mean net worth $1,063,700 in 2022
Largest three-year median net-worth increase in modern SCF history
sources.limitations: Survey-based; top-coded extremes; snapshot years; does not by itself establish causes of concentration.
sources.notes: Preferred primary source for household balance-sheet levels.

sources.title: Distributional Financial Accounts — Distribution of Household Wealth in the U.S. since 1989
authors: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
sources.summary: Quarterly Distributional Financial Accounts integrate SCF microdata with Financial Accounts aggregates. Wealth remains highly concentrated; bottom half of the wealth distribution holds a small share of total wealth.
key_findings: FRED DFA share tables (Q1 2026): top 1% ≈ 28.8% of wealth; 90th–99th ≈ 34.7%; bottom 50% ≈ 5.3%
Implies top decile near ~63.5% of household wealth in that quarter
sources.limitations: Model-based quarterly estimates; methodology differs from SCF point estimates; shares vary by quarter and asset definition.
sources.notes: Use for concentration shares; cross-check with SCF for levels.

sources.title: Understanding the labor productivity and compensation gap
sources.summary: BLS Beyond the Numbers analysis: productivity and compensation rose together for decades after the 1940s, then diverged since the 1970s at aggregate and many industry levels.
key_findings: Documents a productivity–compensation gap since the 1970s
Industry detail shows compensation lagging productivity in most studied industries (1987–2015)
sources.limitations: Measurement choices (deflators, sectors, compensation vs typical-worker pay) affect gap size; article is older than current BLS releases.
sources.notes: Primary federal acknowledgment of divergence phenomenon.

sources.title: The Productivity–Pay Gap
sources.summary: EPI constructs a net-productivity vs typical-worker hourly compensation series from BLS and BEA inputs. Reports large cumulative divergence since 1979 (e.g., net productivity up far more than typical-worker pay).
key_findings: From 1979 to 2020, EPI reports net productivity +61.8% vs typical-worker hourly pay +17.5% (inflation-adjusted), per their methodology page
sources.limitations: Advocacy-affiliated research institute; series construction choices (typical worker definition, net productivity) are contested; not a federal official series.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Progressive labor-oriented think tank — use alongside BLS primary series, not alone.
sources.notes: Secondary synthesis; preserve as one perspective on the gap.

sources.title: Economic Census 2022 — Concentration of Largest Firms (EC2200SIZECONCEN)
sources.summary: Official Economic Census establishment/firm-size concentration ratios (CR4/CR8/CR20/CR50 and related measures) for U.S. industries.
key_findings: Provides industry-level concentration ratios for 2022 Economic Census
Enables tracking of largest-firm shares of sales/shipments/revenue
sources.limitations: Industry definitions and national aggregation; concentration ≠ proven market power; not a single economy-wide monopoly index.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Official Census Bureau Economic Census product.
sources.notes: Primary source for competition domain architecture.

sources.title: Does employee ownership improve performance?
sources.summary: IZA World of Labor synthesis: over 100 studies generally link employee ownership to better productivity, pay, job stability, and survival on average; effects are dispersed and causation is difficult to establish firmly. Meta-analysis finds small positive average performance association.
key_findings: Small but significant average positive association with firm performance in meta-analysis (r̄≈0.04 cited)
Free-rider problems may be mitigated by complementary workplace practices
sources.limitations: Selection into ESOPs; heterogeneous designs; publication bias risk; not proof that all ownership forms always improve outcomes.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Academic synthesis; author is a leading EO researcher.
sources.notes: Supports 'can improve' not 'always improves'.

sources.title: Research findings on employee ownership
sources.summary: NCEO research digest summarizing studies associating ESOPs with productivity, retention, and crisis resilience in some samples, including food-industry COVID comparisons.
key_findings: Cites meta-analysis of 102 studies with small positive performance link
Reports ESOP adoption associated with labor-productivity increases in some establishment studies
sources.limitations: Advocacy/membership organization for employee ownership; selection effects; results vary by governance quality.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Pro-employee-ownership nonprofit — pair with independent academic reviews.
sources.notes: Secondary; opposing caveat is selection and small average effects.

sources.title: Rural America at a Glance, 2025 Edition
sources.summary: ERS annual nonmetro overview: ~46.2 million nonmetro residents (13.6% of U.S.) in July 2024; nonmetro growth slower than metro; 51% of nonmetro counties declined 2020–2024 despite aggregate nonmetro gains from migration.
key_findings: Nonmetro population 46.2 million (July 2024), 13.6% of U.S.
51% of nonmetro counties lost population July 2020–June 2024
sources.limitations: County typology and metro adjacency matter; aggregate nonmetro gains mask widespread county decline.
sources.notes: Primary rural demography source.

sources.title: 146 rural hospitals closed or stopped providing inpatient services from 2005 to 2023
sources.summary: ERS chart note: 146 rural-county hospitals closed or converted from acute inpatient care (2005–2023); 81 shut down completely; financial stress is primary driver.
key_findings: 146 closures/conversions 2005–2023
81 complete shutdowns
sources.limitations: Does not measure access minutes for all communities; conversion still leaves some services.
sources.notes: Healthcare access proxy for rural resilience.

sources.title: Long-Term Trends in Rural Depopulation and Their Implications for Community Banks
sources.summary: FDIC analysis: more than half of rural counties lost population 1980–2010; community bank charters in depopulating rural areas declined sharply with industry consolidation.
key_findings: Over half of rural counties lost population 1980–2010
Community bank charters in depopulating rural areas fell substantially 1984–2012
sources.limitations: Older article; banking structure has continued to change; does not prove causation from depopulation alone.
sources.notes: Historical structural context for local capital access.

sources.title: Earnings, Income, and Wealth Inequality in America: New Evidence from the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances (NBER WP 33823)
sources.summary: NBER working paper on 2022 SCF: wealth remains highly concentrated; reports top 1% holding about 35% of wealth in 2022, down from a 2016 peak near 39%, with housing gains benefiting middle-class households.
key_findings: Top 1% wealth share ≈35% in 2022 SCF analysis (paper)
Concentration declined modestly from mid-2010s peak while remaining high
sources.limitations: Working paper (not peer-reviewed final); estimates depend on SCF processing choices; differs from DFA quarterly shares.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Academic working paper — secondary to Fed SCF bulletin.
sources.notes: Use as secondary corroboration; prefer Fed SCF/DFA for official citation.

sources.title: FRED — Shares of Wealth by Wealth Percentile Groups (Distributional Financial Accounts)
authors: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis / Board of Governors
sources.summary: FRED release tables for DFA wealth shares by percentile groups.
sources.limitations: Quarterly model-based shares; subject to revision.
sources.notes: Canonical share figures for baseline metrics.

sources.title: The Distribution of Household Income in 2021
sources.summary: CBO distributional analysis of household income, means-tested transfers, and federal taxes for 2021. Highest-quintile average income before transfers/taxes roughly 19× lowest quintile; after transfers and taxes about 7×. Federal taxes and transfers reduce measured inequality but do not eliminate concentration of income and tax payments at the top.
key_findings: Highest-quintile average income before transfers/taxes ≈19× lowest quintile in 2021
After transfers and taxes, highest/lowest ratio ≈7×
Pandemic-era transfers and credits raised lower-income incomes while capital gains raised top incomes
sources.limitations: CBO income/tax concepts differ from IRS AGI or SCF wealth; 2021 includes temporary pandemic policies; incidence assumptions are model-based.
sources.notes: Primary federal source for income/tax distribution architecture.

sources.title: Rucho v. Common Cause, 588 U.S. ___ (2019)
authors: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.summary: Holding: partisan-gerrymandering claims present political questions beyond the reach of federal courts. Leaves substantial reform pathways to Congress, state constitutions and courts, commissions, and voters.
key_findings: Partisan gerrymandering claims held nonjusticiable in federal courts as political questions
Does not authorize partisan gerrymandering; channels remedies largely outside federal judicial policing of partisan maps
sources.limitations: Legal holding, not an empirical map-fairness study; state and congressional avenues remain; racial vote-dilution doctrines are distinct.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: U.S. Supreme Court majority opinion; dissent exists and should be read for contrary constitutional theory.
sources.notes: Primary legal context for redistricting reform architecture.

sources.title: Redistricting Commissions: State Legislative Plans
sources.summary: NCSL overview of state redistricting commission and related nonlegislative arrangements for state legislative plans; structures and independence vary by state.
key_findings: Multiple states use commissions or other nonlegislative arrangements
Commission design and independence are not uniform
sources.limitations: Secondary institutional summary; verify against state constitutions/statutes for any specific state claim.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Bipartisan state legislative association research/service organization.
sources.notes: Use for institutional variation; not a single national commission mandate.

sources.title: Legislative Term Limits: An Overview
sources.summary: NCSL overview of state legislative term limits. A minority of states use them; literature and experience include both rotation-of-power aims and concerns that influence can shift toward lobbyists, staff, agencies, and party organizations when legislative institutional knowledge declines.
key_findings: Sixteen states currently have legislative term limits (per NCSL overview context)
Term limits are not a complete anti-capture solution
sources.limitations: Secondary overview; effects vary by state design; count and details should be re-checked against current NCSL tables before publication of exact tallies.
sources.notes: Supports caution against treating term limits as sufficient officeholder-integrity design.

sources.title: Community Policing Defined
authors: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Community Oriented Policing Services (COPS Office)
sources.summary: Defines community policing as organizational strategies supporting partnerships and problem-solving to address conditions that give rise to crime, social disorder, and fear of crime. Identifies three key components: Community Partnerships, Organizational Transformation, and Problem Solving.
key_findings: Community policing comprises Community Partnerships, Organizational Transformation, and Problem Solving
Police rarely can solve public safety problems alone; interactive partnerships with stakeholders are central
sources.limitations: Philosophical/operational definition document, not an outcome evaluation of a specific local Community Safety Corps design.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: DOJ COPS Office publication defining federal community-policing vocabulary.
sources.notes: Foundation for carrying community-policing elements further into a complete Community Safety Corps architecture.

sources.title: Phasing Out Our Use of Private Prisons
authors: Sally Q. Yates, Deputy Attorney General (U.S. Department of Justice)
sources.summary: DOJ announcement accompanying the August 18, 2016 Yates memorandum directing the Bureau of Prisons to reduce and ultimately end the use of privately operated prisons, citing concerns including safety and correctional services compared with BOP facilities.
key_findings: 2016 DOJ directive sought to reduce and phase out privately operated federal prisons
Rationale cited comparative concerns about privately operated facilities
sources.limitations: Federal BOP contracting posture only; does not itself settle state/local private-jail or private-probation rules; later rescinded (see CC-SRC-019).
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Obama-administration DOJ policy; superseded by later administrations.
sources.notes: Use with CC-SRC-019 to document private-prison policy instability across administrations — not as an invented national privatization prevalence statistic.

sources.title: Memorandum: Rescission of Memorandum on Use of Private Prisons
authors: Jefferson B. Sessions III, Attorney General (U.S. Department of Justice)
sources.summary: February 21, 2017 Attorney General memorandum rescinding the August 18, 2016 Yates memorandum and directing that the Department will continue to use private prisons as needed.
key_findings: 2017 Sessions memorandum rescinded the 2016 Yates private-prison phase-down directive
Illustrates that federal private-prison contracting policy can reverse across administrations
sources.limitations: Federal BOP policy only; later executive orders and contracting decisions may further change posture; does not quantify state/local private corrections markets.
sources.ideological_or_institutional_considerati: Trump-administration DOJ policy reversing prior directive.
sources.notes: Corrects informal claims that a 2023 memorandum was the rescission; the documented rescission of the Yates memo is the 2017 Sessions memo. Later EO/policy churn reinforces the case for settling principle in law.

sources.title: Adult Treatment Court Program | Overview
authors: Bureau of Justice Assistance, Office of Justice Programs
sources.summary: BJA overview of federal support for adult treatment courts. Notes DOJ has supported treatment courts for decades; programs integrate evidence-based substance-use treatment, testing, sanctions and incentives, and recovery support under judicial supervision. Outcomes depend on program design and implementation.
key_findings: Federal justice agencies have long supported adult treatment-court models
Model elements include treatment, testing, sanctions/incentives, and recovery supports in supervised court settings
sources.limitations: Program overview, not a meta-analysis guaranteeing uniform recidivism reductions; quality varies by local design.
sources.notes: Supports Path C (addiction-driven conduct) as an evidence-informed option, not a universal mandate.

sources.title: Mental health courts
authors: Bureau of Justice Assistance, Office of Justice Programs
sources.summary: BJA taxonomy/resource hub recognizing mental health courts and related justice–behavioral-health collaboration for people with mental illness or co-occurring substance-use disorders.
key_findings: Federal justice programming recognizes specialized mental-health court and collaboration models
Behavioral-health and justice systems are treated as linked for relevant populations
sources.limitations: Taxonomy/resource page, not a single outcome study; does not prescribe a specific Community Safety Corps staffing model.
sources.notes: Supports Path D (mental-health crisis) collaboration framing.

sources.title: Recidivism
sources.summary: NIJ topic page on recidivism as a core justice-system measure. Emphasizes that measurement choices matter; rearrest, reconviction, and reincarceration capture different outcomes.
key_findings: Recidivism is a fundamental corrections/justice measure
Definition and measurement (rearrest vs reconviction vs reincarceration) affect interpretation
sources.limitations: Topic overview, not a single national rate claim; do not invent national recidivism percentages from this page alone.
sources.notes: Supports careful recidivism reporting for restoration campuses.

sources.title: Five Things About Reentry
sources.summary: NIJ brief describing reentry as a continuum from intake assessment and in-custody programming through release planning, supervision, and community reintegration. Stresses individualized, holistic supports and nuanced success measures beyond rearrest alone.
key_findings: Reentry is a continuum beginning during confinement, not only at the gate
Programs and services should be tailored; holistic supports matter
Success metrics should be more nuanced than rearrest alone
sources.limitations: Research synthesis brief; does not guarantee that any particular local reentry package will succeed.
sources.notes: Supports reentry-from-day-one doctrine without overclaiming outcomes.

sources.title: Impact of Prison Reentry Services on Short-Term Outcomes: Evidence From a Multisite Evaluation
sources.summary: NIJ-hosted multisite evaluation evidence on short-term outcomes of prison reentry services. Findings are mixed/modest in areas often including employment, housing, service access, and substance use rather than magical uniform success — supporting rigorous evaluation rather than blanket claims that every reentry service works.
key_findings: Reentry-service effects on short-term outcomes are not uniformly large
Supports cautious, evaluation-driven reentry policy
sources.limitations: Study vintage and sites limit generalizability; short-term outcomes are not lifetime success; read full report before citing specific effect sizes.
sources.notes: Use as evidence caution against overclaiming reentry program effectiveness.
